content:
Hi everyone, first post here. Hoping to solicit some ideas for my research and connect with anyone who's interested.

I'm working on premise selection for Lean. In the abstract, a good premise to use after a proof state is one that finishes the proof or leads to finishing the proof. But generating lots of alternate proofs at scale is expensive, so I'm in search of cheap ways to evaluate the 'relevance' of a premise to a proof state.

What I've tried so far:

  1. Just ask Claude Opus 5. It's pretty good on a test set I have! But it doesn't scale cheaply enough for my budget.
  2. I used a dumb template:
return [
f"exact {p}",
f"fail_if_no_progress (apply {p})",
f"fail_if_no_progress (rw [{p}])",
f"fail_if_no_progress (rw [← {p}])",
f"((try simp only []); fail_if_no_progress (simp only [{p}]))",
]

This worked maybe a quarter of the time, according to my noisy evaluation of this. I would follow this with the fail_if_no_progress tactic https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Tactic/FailIfNoProgress.html just to make sure the progress wasn't simple. But there are trivial premises that always run, like some inequality premises that can run on any proof state with an inequality in it.

  1. There are tactic generation models that are retrieval aware, like ReProver and REAL Prover. ReProver is a little small and dumb, so it didn't output useful tactics often. REAL Prover is bigger and ostensibly smarter, but its outputs have been surprisingly garbled for me.

Anyway, I was hoping to solicit feedback and new ideas from other people online and connect with people who are interested in this topic. Thanks for reading!
Just out of curiosity, why LeanPremise does not do the job for what you have in mind?
